claims.text: The initial alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution with a random atomic distribution.
Controlled solutionizing and aging can systematically increase chemical short-range order.
Controlled thermal aging can systematically increase local lattice distortions.
The proposed thermal treatments can increase ordering and distortion without changing composition or introducing secondary phases.
Chemical short-range-order clusters occur as local atomic-scale features in multicomponent concentrated alloys.
Chemical short-range order is associated with local lattice distortions.
Chemical ordering and its local lattice strain fields create barriers to dislocation motion.
Increasing chemical short-range order increases the activation stress required for dislocation glide.
Stronger barriers to dislocation motion increase yield strength.
Increased chemical ordering modifies the dominant deformation mode.
Ordering-induced barriers may promote deformation channels other than ordinary dislocation glide.
More highly ordered specimens will have systematically higher yield strength than minimally ordered, as-solutionized specimens.
More highly ordered specimens will exhibit altered dislocation activity relative to the baseline.
Increased ordering may change twinning or deformation-localization behavior.
The proposed mechanism applies where dislocation-mediated plasticity dominates and secondary phases are absent.
The deformation response of multicomponent concentrated alloys can vary at elevated temperature.
The magnitude of ordering-related strengthening may depend on alloy system, aging conditions, temperature, and strain rate.
Twinning or phase transformation may compete with the proposed dislocation-barrier mechanism.

contradictions.description: The falsification design describes the two sample sets as having identical processing histories, but one set receives an additional aging treatment; only their histories prior to the intervention can be identical.
